ACTIONS SELF-HOSTED EXPOSURE CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your self-hosted GitHub Actions runner exposed to a fork?

GitHub's own documentation says not to use self-hosted runners on public repositories — a workflow triggered by pull_request runs the workflow file from the pull request's own branch, so a fork's author can add their own steps and have them execute directly on your runner machine. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds every job that runs on a self-hosted label inside a workflow triggered by pull_request, pull_request_target, workflow_run, or issue_comment.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineJobStatusDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any fork-exposed job is found

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added exposed job before it merges.

Common questions

Why is a self-hosted runner risky on a public repository?

GitHub's own documentation recommends against using self-hosted runners on public repositories, because a workflow triggered by pull_request runs the workflow file from the pull request's own branch. Anyone who can open a PR against your repository can edit that workflow file and have their own steps execute directly on your runner machine.

Is pull_request_target or workflow_run just as risky as pull_request?

Differently risky. pull_request_target and workflow_run always run the workflow file from your base branch, not the fork's, so a stranger cannot rewrite the steps that execute. But both still respond to a fork-influenced event, often with repository secrets available, and a self-hosted job that also checks out and builds the fork's code still runs that code on infrastructure you own rather than an ephemeral GitHub-hosted VM. This tool flags all four risky triggers and names which one matched so you can judge the specific case.

Does this tool know whether my repository is actually public?

No. It makes no network calls of any kind and never checks your repository's visibility, required-approval settings, or whether an organization runner group is actually self-hosted. It flags the pattern in the workflow file; whether that pattern is actually exploitable on your repository is for you to confirm.

Does a clean scan mean my self-hosted runners are safe?

No. This checks one specific, narrow pattern: the literal self-hosted label combined with one of four documented risky triggers. It does not evaluate runner group names, network segmentation, ephemeral vs persistent runners, or anything about how the runner machine itself is hardened.

What should I do about a flagged job?

Move the job to a GitHub-hosted runner, restrict the workflow's trigger to events a fork cannot raise (push to a protected branch, workflow_dispatch, schedule), or require manual approval for every workflow run from an outside collaborator — GitHub's own setting for this is under Settings → Actions → General → "Fork pull request workflows".

More: why self-hosted runners and public repositories don't mix, and how to fix it.

Already using a runtime monitor on your runners? See this checker vs. StepSecurity's Harden-Runner.

Reviewing workflow files yourself instead? See this checker vs. reviewing workflows by eye.

self-hosted-runners-in-public-repositori.text:
← Actions Self-Hosted Exposure Check

Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners and public repositories don't mix

A workflow triggered by pull_request runs the workflow file as it exists on the pull request's own branch, not your base branch. If a job in that workflow runs on a self-hosted label, the pull request's author controls the steps that execute on your runner machine.

Most self-hosted setups start innocently: a repository needs a GPU, a licensed compiler, or access to an internal network that a GitHub-hosted VM cannot reach, so a job gets runs-on: self-hosted.

name: build
on: pull_request
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./build.sh

On a private repository, every contributor is already trusted, so this is fine. On a public repository, anyone can open a pull request — and because the trigger is plain pull_request, GitHub runs the version of this workflow file committed on the pull request's own branch. The fork's author can rewrite the steps: entirely: read files on the runner, reach whatever network the runner can reach, or install a persistent backdoor if the runner is not rebuilt between jobs.

1. Prefer a GitHub-hosted runner whenever the job allows it

If the job does not genuinely need something only your own machine has, move it back to a GitHub-hosted label:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

Each GitHub-hosted job runs in a fresh, ephemeral VM, so there is no persistent machine for a fork's workflow to compromise.

2. If you genuinely need self-hosted, restrict the trigger

Keep the self-hosted job, but move it off a trigger a fork can raise. A push to a branch only your own collaborators can push to, or a manual dispatch, does not hand a stranger control:

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

3. Require approval for fork pull requests

GitHub's own setting under Settings → Actions → General → "Fork pull request workflows" can require a maintainer to approve every run from an outside contributor, or from anyone who is not already a known collaborator. This does not change what a workflow file could do once approved — it adds a human checkpoint before a fork's code ever reaches the runner.

4. pull_request_target and workflow_run are a different, still real, risk

These two triggers always run the workflow file from your base branch, so a fork cannot rewrite the steps. But they still respond to fork-influenced events, often with repository secrets available to the job, and a self-hosted runner combined with a step that checks out and executes the fork's own code (the "pwn request" pattern) still runs that code on infrastructure you own rather than a disposable VM. If a self-hosted job under one of these triggers also checks out an untrusted head, treat it with the same seriousness as plain pull_request.

5. Check every workflow at once

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Self-Hosted Exposure Check to find every job that runs on a self-hosted label under one of the four risky triggers, across every file at once — or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any job is fork-exposed by this tool's definition — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added exposed job before it merges.

What this does not tell you

This tool cannot see whether your repository is actually public, whether required-approval settings are already on, or whether a named runner group (runs-on: {group: ...}) is self-hosted — it flags only the literal self-hosted label. A clean scan is not a claim that your self-hosted infrastructure is otherwise hardened.

Everything on the linked tool runs in your browser; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool makes no network calls of its own.

vs-reviewing-workflows-by-eye.html.text:
← Actions Self-Hosted Exposure Check

Actions Self-Hosted Exposure Check vs. reviewing workflows by eye

Reading a workflow file for a self-hosted runner under a risky trigger is a real skill, and an experienced reviewer catches the obvious case every time. This page names no product or company -- "reviewing by eye" is the generic habit every maintainer already has, not a competing tool.

Where a careful read holds up, and where it slips

A job with runs-on: self-hosted sitting right below an on: pull_request_target trigger is easy to spot once you know the shape. What's harder to hold in your head while scanning a real repository's workflow files: self-hosted can show up as one label among several in a runs-on: list rather than the whole value; workflow_run and issue_comment carry the same fork-influenced risk as pull_request_target without "pull request" in the name to cue the reviewer; a second job further down the same file can have its own, different runs-on: after the first job already looked clean; and a runner group or a ${{ }} matrix expression can't be judged safe or unsafe from the file text at all, which is easy to either wave through or flag on a hunch.

Where to answer each question.
CaseReviewing by eyeThis tool
Bare runs-on: self-hosted under pull_request_targetEasy to catchCatches it the same way
runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64] under the same triggerEasy to miss when self-hosted is one item in a list rather than the whole lineParses every label in flow-list, block-list, or single-value form
Trigger is workflow_run or issue_comment rather than pull_request_targetEasy to read past -- review habit is trained on pull_request_target, and neither name says "pull request"Checked against the same fixed four-trigger set regardless of which one is top of mind
A second job further down the same workflow file, with its own runs-on:Easy to skip once the first job in the file already looked cleanEvery job block in the file is found and classified independently
runs-on: selects a runner group by nameEasy to guess safe or unsafe from the group's name aloneReported honestly as unclassifiable from this file, not guessed either way
runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }} (a matrix expression)Easy to wave through since it doesn't literally say self-hostedFlagged as unable to classify statically rather than silently passed as safe
A repository with a dozen workflow filesRe-reading all of them, every time a workflow changes, is tedious and easy to shortcutPaste as many files as you have, or run check.py across a whole checked-out repository
Blocking a newly-added finding before it mergesDepends on a human noticing it in reviewcheck.py --fail-on-risk gives a real exit code from the same classification, wired into your own CI

The two are complementary, not competing: this tool does not decide whether a flagged job is actually reachable from an attacker in your specific setup, or whether the repository is even public -- it makes no network calls and never checks that. It replaces the tedious, error-prone part of the read-through: finding every job in every file, parsing every runs-on: form, and checking each one against the same fixed trigger list every time.

Run the free self-hosted exposure check

Common questions

What does reviewing a workflow for self-hosted exposure by eye actually catch?

A reviewer who knows the pattern will catch the obvious case: a job with runs-on: self-hosted sitting a few lines below an on: pull_request_target trigger. That recognition is real, and this tool checks the same underlying combination -- a self-hosted label and one of four documented risky triggers -- rather than a wider or different rule.

Why is self-hosted easy to miss when it's inside a runs-on: list?

runs-on: can be a single label, a flow-style list like runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64], or a block list with one label per line. A reviewer scanning quickly for the literal line runs-on: self-hosted can walk right past self-hosted when it's the first of three items in a list, especially when the eye lands on a more distinctive label like linux or x64 first. This tool parses every label in the list, in any of the three forms, and matches self-hosted as one item among several rather than expecting the whole value to equal that one word.

Why are workflow_run and issue_comment easy to forget as risky triggers?

Most self-hosted-exposure review habit is trained on pull_request_target, because that trigger's whole reputation is built on the pwn-request pattern. workflow_run and issue_comment do not have "pull request" in the name, so a reviewer scanning a workflow's on: block for the familiar trigger can read past both without recognizing that they hand a stranger the same kind of influence GitHub's own guidance already names. This tool checks a job's runs-on: against the same fixed set of four triggers regardless of which one happens to be top of mind that day, and names the specific trigger that matched in its output.

Why is a second job in the same workflow file easy to miss?

A reviewer who reads the first job in a file, confirms its runs-on: is safe, and moves on to the next file can stop reading before a second job further down the same file -- one with its own, different runs-on: line. This tool finds every job block in a file independently and classifies each one on its own runs-on:, so a risky second job is reported even when the first job in the same file is clean.

Does a clean result from this tool mean my self-hosted runners are safe?

No. It checks one specific, narrow pattern in the workflow files you give it: the literal self-hosted label combined with one of four documented risky triggers, in the jobs it can classify statically. A runs-on: that selects a runner group by name, or one built from a ${{ }} matrix expression, is reported honestly as unclassifiable from the file alone rather than guessed either way -- and it makes no network call, so it never knows whether the repository the workflow lives in is actually public.

vs-stepsecurity.html.text:
← Actions self-hosted exposure check

This checker vs. StepSecurity Harden-Runner

Harden-Runner, from StepSecurity, is a GitHub Action you add as a step inside a job. While that job runs, it monitors the job's outbound network calls and file integrity, and can flag or block egress that was not expected -- a runtime control that watches one job for the duration it actually executes on the runner.

This checker does not run a job at all. It is a free, zero-dependency tool -- usable in the browser or as a stdlib-only Python CLI -- that reads your .github/workflows/*.yml files as text and flags every job whose runs-on includes the literal self-hosted label and whose triggering event is pull_request, pull_request_target, workflow_run, or issue_comment -- the exact combination GitHub's own documentation names as a reason not to use self-hosted runners on a public repository -- and prints which trigger matched. Nothing about it needs a job to run first.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Monitor and constrain what a specific job actually does -- network calls, file writes -- while it runs on your infrastructure. Harden-Runner -- that is precisely its job, as a step inside the workflow it is watching.
Find out, before any job has ever run, which workflow files pair a self-hosted runner with a trigger a fork can raise. This checker -- a text scan of your workflow YAML, no job execution needed.
Audit a whole repository's workflow files in CI with a single exit code, no action installed into the workflows themselves. This checker's CLI -- python3 check.py --fail-on-risk, stdlib only.
Get an allowlist of expected network endpoints and be alerted on anything outside it during a run. Harden-Runner -- this checker makes no claim about runtime network behavior at all.
Decide whether a newly-opened workflow file is safe to merge before it ever executes on a self-hosted runner. This checker -- it reads the file as committed; nothing has to run first.

These sit at different points in the same job's life rather than competing for the same one. This checker is a cheap, static gate on the workflow files themselves -- run it in CI on every pull request that touches .github/workflows/ -- and Harden-Runner is a runtime control for the jobs you have decided should run. A team that wants both exposure classes covered reasonably runs this checker first and Harden-Runner on the jobs it lets through.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or StepSecurity's Harden-Runner?

They act at different moments and most teams taking self-hosted-runner exposure seriously will want both. Harden-Runner, from StepSecurity, is a GitHub Action you add as a step inside a job; while that job runs, it monitors outbound network calls and file integrity and can block or flag unexpected egress -- a runtime control, watching one job as it actually executes. This checker never runs a job at all. It is a free, zero-dependency scanner (browser or CLI) that reads your .github/workflows/*.yml files as text and flags every job that combines a self-hosted runner label with pull_request, pull_request_target, workflow_run, or issue_comment -- GitHub's own documented risky combination -- before that job is ever scheduled. Reach for Harden-Runner to monitor and constrain what a job does while it runs. Reach for this to catch the exposed combination in your workflow files themselves, including ones that have not run yet.

If Harden-Runner already monitors the runner, why check the workflow file too?

Because a runtime monitor only sees a job once it starts, and by definition a self-hosted runner triggered by a forked pull_request has already let a stranger's workflow-file edits reach your machine by the time any step -- Harden-Runner included -- begins executing. Reading the workflow YAML directly catches the exposed trigger-plus-label combination itself, as a static fact about the file, whether or not the job has ever run. The two are complementary rather than redundant: this checker is about whether a job should be reachable by a fork at all; Harden-Runner is about constraining what that job can do once it is.

Is Harden-Runner free too? What does this add?

Being free is not the difference, and this page does not claim it is: StepSecurity offers Harden-Runner as a GitHub Action available to add to a workflow. The difference is shape and scope. Harden-Runner instruments a running job and needs to be added, per job, to the workflows you want it watching. This checker needs nothing added to your workflows at all -- point the CLI at a checkout, or paste YAML into the browser tool, and it reads the files as they already are, with no network call and nothing installed into your CI. It is built for the moment before a job runs, which a runtime action by definition cannot cover.

Is this page affiliated with StepSecurity?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by StepSecurity, Inc., and Harden-Runner and StepSecurity are named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. The description of Harden-Runner on this page is drawn from StepSecurity's own public documentation; check it there for what the action currently monitors and how.
